text: This lesson looks at a specific, common cause of slow forms: too many UI Policies evaluating at once. You already know UI Policies from the admin view and from the deeper developer mechanics earlier in this path — now we're looking at what happens when a form accumulates far too many of them.

A single UI Policy evaluating on form load is genuinely cheap — the platform checks one condition and applies a small set of field changes. The problem shows up at scale. A form that's picked up ten, twenty, or more active UI Policies over years of incremental customization asks the platform to evaluate every one of those conditions on every single load — even ones governing a field nobody uses anymore. Each check is small. The sum of dozens of them, every load, is not.

The risk escalates sharply with a UI Policy that has Run Scripts enabled, because that lets the policy execute real client-side JavaScript the moment its condition is true. A quick script is fine. But a UI Policy running an expensive onCondition function — looping over related records, making a synchronous GlideRecord call, heavy DOM work — is doing meaningfully more than a declarative field-state change, and it's doing that work on the critical path of the form becoming usable.

Once the Slow Request Log has confirmed a form is genuinely slow, the next real step is reviewing the UI Policies that govern it. Count how many are actually active. Ask of each one: is it still needed, does it duplicate another policy's logic, and if it has Run Scripts enabled, is that script doing anything that's genuinely expensive, or could it be simplified to a declarative setting instead?

This kind of overload is a pattern, not a one-time accident. Every new requirement tends to add one more policy rather than revisiting whether an existing one could be extended or retired. Left unchecked across many forms, that's exactly how an instance ends up with widespread, hard-to-explain slowness that no single change seems to fix — because it was never one big problem, it was dozens of small ones added up.

Reviewing UI Policies for redundancy and expensive scripts is usually about removing or consolidating, not rewriting anything clever. Next, we'll turn to list views and Related Lists, and what makes a list slow to render.
